div.style: color: rgb(255, 255, 255) !important; display: table; white-space: break-spaces; line-height: 1.5; max-width: 820px; text-align: center; width: 820px;

span.p:
Fixed design prompt (prompts/designer_prompt.txt — never changes)
You are a world-class book cover designer. Design 4 complete front cover for the book below, they should be all very different.
What makes a world-class cover:
- ONE single strong idea — image and type together reduce to one concept you can name in a sentence. Never decoration.
- A visual metaphor that lands instantly but rewards a second look.
- Works as a tiny thumbnail AND from across a room — bold, simple, high contrast.
- A disciplined palette (one dominant colour + one accent) and real negative space.
- Typography is part of the design, not a label: clear hierarchy — title dominant, author secondary, any tagline smallest.
- The genre's visual code, plus exactly one twist that sparks curiosity.
- Above all: it must sell and become the book's identity.
Put on the FRONT: the title (the Book title in the facts) and nothing else, apart from the footer below. No author, no subtitle, no tagline, no other text.
Do NOT put the publisher logo on the front — that belongs on the spine and back cover.
A) Render the type on the cover: integrate the title as designed typography.
Footer (the same on every cover): along the very bottom of the cover, a straight ribbon banner running the full width, flush against the left and right edges, with small swallow-tail notches at both ends, about 10% of the cover height. The ribbon is filled saffron-gold with dark text. On two lines, centred: first the exact text "Practical Gita" in a classical serif, letter-spaced, as the larger line; below it the exact pillar name from the facts (the Pillar line), for example "Know yourself", in a clean sans-serif at about 40% of the size above. The footer is identical in shape, position and typography on all 4 covers; only the artwork above it differs. Compose each cover so the ribbon feels part of the design and not stuck on, and keep the title clear of it.

span.p:
Book facts (changes per insight)
Book title: Overwhelmed? This Is How Strong People Deal With It.
Pillar: Know yourself
Genre: Self-Help / Personal Development / Applied Philosophy
Target Audience: High achievers, professionals, leaders and anyone dealing with stress and overwhelm, as well as low mood and a sense of emptiness, seeking self-awareness, resilience and self-acceptance through a blend of psychology and ancient wisdom.

div.style: color: rgb(255, 255, 255) !important; display: table; white-space: break-spaces; line-height: 1.5; max-width: 820px; text-align: center; width: 820px;

span.p:
Synopsis (the insight body, as is — changes per insight)
Ever look at someone and think, "Wow, that person is so strong nothing can touch them!"? That's exactly who Arjuna was to all his brothers-in-arms. He had led them to victory multiple times through intense turmoil. But, on the fateful day of the Great War, upon gazing around the battlefield of Kurukshetra, a sense of dread and uncertainty took over Arjuna. He saw his own family—uncles, cousins, teachers, friends—on both sides of the battlefield. Ready to kill or be killed by each other. His mind starts to reel: "How can I fight those I love?" "What's the use of winning this war if it means destroying my family?" Overwhelmed by grief and confusion, he famously let his bow drop, declaring, "I cannot fight." Let's step into a (relatively) more modern setting for a moment. Winston Churchill, Britain's wartime leader, candidly admitted to what he called his "Black Dog"—his recurring, paralyzing depression. Despite being the figurehead of courage, Churchill repeatedly found himself frozen by an emotional storm within. Psychology explains why high performers crack. Performance rises with arousal only up to a point; push past that and it falls off a cliff—the Yerkes–Dodson curve. In overload, the brain's prefrontal cortex (planning, perspective, impulse control) goes offline, so even experts freeze or fixate. Strength doesn't erase vulnerability; greatness doesn't shield from profound despair. Like Arjuna, Churchill's battles weren't just external—they were intensely internal. The point we are trying to make is this: No one is immune to emotional overwhelm—not even the most capable and courageous. Vulnerability is part of the human experience. Your breaking point is not the end. It's the beginning of self-acceptance and real strength. Bhagavad Gita's story starts with Arjuna's collapse, not conquest. So does most real growth.

span.p:
Image prompt (Gemini's output — 4 concepts, one shown below)
Cover 1: The Shattered Armor
A stark, high-contrast book cover in a minimalist style, featuring a large, solid-black, ancient warrior's helmet centered on a pure, bone-white background. Running down the exact center of the helmet is a single, glowing, vivid neon-blue crack, symbolizing the breaking point of the strong. The book title "Overwhelmed?" is integrated directly into the design, rendered in a bold, elegant, black sans-serif font positioned prominently above the helmet, with "This Is How Strong People Deal With It." set in smaller, clean, light-weight typography beneath it. The color palette is strictly bone-white, black, and neon-blue. Along the very bottom of the cover, flush against the left and right edges, is a straight ribbon banner running the full width, about 10% of the cover height. The ribbon has small swallow-tail notches at both ends and is filled with a solid saffron-gold color containing dark text. Centered on the ribbon in two lines is the text: first, "Practical Gita" in a classical serif, widely letter-spaced, as the larger line; below it, "Know yourself" in a clean sans-serif at about 40% of the size above.
(...plus Cover 2: The Fallen Bow, Cover 3: The Heavy Crown, Cover 4: The Yerkes-Dodson Wave — each a full paragraph like this, same footer repeated)
